messages.subject: Running TITAN on tetraploid samples
parts:
Dear Gavin,

I am trying to run TITAN on a set of samples where I know the approximate ploidy state for many is around 3 to 4. I have run TITAN following your instructions to set ploidy to 4, but in the output the algorithm seem to call the entire genome as aberrant. While there is an argument for calling anything beyond diploid as aberrant, I would rather opt for deviation from the ploidy. 
Is there a way to change how Titan is calling aberrations? Or is this mainly an annotation issue, which would not affect the algorithms performance, so it may not be an issue if I just ignore this column?
Or do you have a more specific suggestion to handling polyploid samples, including optimizing for the correct ploidy/cellularity?

Also, in the results output, when there are less than three subclones called, I get the copy number for each subclone. However, with 3+ clones, I only get the TITAN copy number and the cluster assignment. How do I from this infer the copy number state of the individual clones? Sorry if this is already in the annotations somewhere, I have been unable to find it so far.

Hope you can help me!

Best, 

Nicolai Birkbak
Research Associate, The Francis Crick Institute, London, UK

messages.author: 71cefeaaa3659875
messages.subject: Re: Running TITAN on tetraploid samples
parts:
Hi Nicolai,

Thanks for your interest in TITAN.

TitanCNA returns the absolute integer copy number.  Thus, when initializing the ploidy to tetraploid (i.e. phi_0 = 4), if the converged ploidy is also around 4, then the you can expect the results to have largely copy number calls near 4 copies.  The ploidy value is defined here as the average tumour ploidy and will correspond to the amount and amplitude of aneuploidy in the genome.  

For your analysis, I think you can simply take the integer copy number prediction and normalize by the rounded value of the predicted ploidy.  That is, you are taking the copy number change relative to euploid.  It really depends if you care for the absolute number of copies or the relative differences compared to the genome's baseline (euploid).  Of course, the challenge will be the case of, say, ploidy = 2.5.  Is this a diploid genome with many amplifications?  Or is this a triploid genome with many deletions?  

TitanCNA only returns subclone1 and subclone2 outputs for < 3 clonal clusters, because it is not always straightforward to determine, from bulk tumour sequencing, the set of events that are truly shared within individual cells of clones.  For example, in a 3 cluster solution, if 2 events with 30% cellular prevalence are clustered in the same "clonal cluster", it is likely they belong to the same clone; however, we cannot rule out the possibility that they may be mutually exclusive in two 30% subclones.  You can imagine using pigeon-hole-like principles to resolve some of these possibilities. Alternatively, analyzing multiple related samples from the same patient can further tease out co-occurrences.  For single bulk tumour samples, there are tools that combine both copy number and point mutations, such as PhyloWGS (Deshwar et al. 2015. Genome Biology, 16:35), that might be useful to look into.

Hope this helps.

Best,
Gavin

parts:
Thanks Gavin, this is very helpful.

I'll do the ploidy transformation you suggest. 
For the >2 clonal clusters cases, I understand how it can be impossible to tease out the exact CN per clone. But just to understand the output then, Titan returns a result per input SNP, each assigned to a clonal cluster. When one SNP is assigned e.g. cluster 4 with an integer CN of 3 and a CCF of 0.25, what CN state should I then expect for that position, for the other clones? Should I expect them to be unchanged, i.e. only the changed clones are returned? 

Also, as it is next to impossible to tease out the individual clones copy number when we go to 3+ clones, would it make sense to e.g. run each chromosome independently with just 1 or 2 clusters and then stitch the results together in the end? Then smaller subclones would be ignored, but the composition could potentially be inferred from the different CCF values of the clones for different chromosomes, and one would get the per clone CN.

Best, 

Nicolai

messages.subject: Re: Running TITAN on tetraploid samples
parts:
On Tuesday, November 1, 2016 at 6:52:54 AM UTC-4, Nicolai Juul Birkbak wrote:
Thanks Gavin, this is very helpful.

I'll do the ploidy transformation you suggest. 
For the >2 clonal clusters cases, I understand how it can be impossible to tease out the exact CN per clone. But just to understand the output then, Titan returns a result per input SNP, each assigned to a clonal cluster. When one SNP is assigned e.g. cluster 4 with an integer CN of 3 and a CCF of 0.25, what CN state should I then expect for that position, for the other clones? Should I expect them to be unchanged, i.e. only the changed clones are returned?

Yes, the other clones are assumed to be copy neutral, heterozygous.  This may be a naive assumption because in some instances, there may be multiple CNA states between different clones within the same locus.  I had plans to add this in but have not gotten around to it.

Also, as it is next to impossible to tease out the individual clones copy number when we go to 3+ clones, would it make sense to e.g. run each chromosome independently with just 1 or 2 clusters and then stitch the results together in the end? Then smaller subclones would be ignored, but the composition could potentially be inferred from the different CCF values of the clones for different chromosomes, and one would get the per clone CN.

Currently, TITAN makes the assumption of "punctuated" clonal expansion, whereby multiple CNA events across the genome are present in large, detectable clones.  Your suggestion would relax this assumption a bit so that it is more similar to "gradual" clonal expansion, which would result in many different CCFs.
It is not quite clear to me what you mean by "stitching" the results together to give you per-clone CN.  How would this be different than using the clonal clusters (i.e. cluster of events with similar CCFs), but perhaps initializing with more clusters to account for more CCF values?  That is, how is stitching different than clustering?

Best, 

Nicolai

Thanks Gavin,

What I meant by stitching them together, would be by doing each chromosome one by one, and only with one or two clones. Then one would get the copy number of the main clones, but with different CCF values across the chromosomes which could be used to infer the number of subclones. Not sure this would really work though.

Anyway, thanks for your help, I am trying to compare TITAN to other NGS CN callers at the moment, and they seem to vary a lot. Wether or not that is because the underlying data is noisy I am not sure, but concordance is definitely lower in low purity samples.
